content: Vacuous truth is a concept in first-order logic that applies to conditional statements. A conditional statement is considered vacuously true if the assertion can already be shown to be true (often through axioms) and the condition is logically unrelated to the assertion. This concept is particularly relevant in pure mathematics. For example, the empty product, which states that the result of multiplying no numbers at all is 1, is a vacuous truth. This principle is useful in various mathematical fields, such as probability theory, combinatorics, and power series. Another example is the elementary symmetric polynomial in no variables, which is also defined to be 1. Similarly, the Euler characteristic is one of the finitely additive measures treated in Hadwiger’s theorem, and its definition involves vacuous truth. Outside of mathematics, vacuously true statements can sometimes be misleading. These statements make reasonable assertions about qualified objects that do not actually exist. For instance, a child might claim, I ate every vegetable on my plate, when there were no vegetables on the plate to begin with. The term vacuously true is generally applied to statements of the form P → Q (if P, then Q), where P is false. Other forms include statements like ∀x, P(x) → Q(x) (for all x, if P(x), then Q(x)), where P(x) is false for all x, or ∀x ∈ A, Q(x) (for all x in set A, Q(x)), where the set A is empty. These forms can often be reduced to the first case with appropriate transformations. Vacuous truth is most commonly applied in classical logic, which is two-valued (true or false). However, it also appears in intuitionistic logic under similar conditions. The case of P → Q where P is false often strikes people as counterintuitive. It is not immediately obvious whether such statements are always true, always false, or sometimes true and sometimes false. For example, consider the statement, If I am in Massachusetts, then I am in North America. Even if one is not currently in Massachusetts, the statement seems reasonable and true. This suggests that at least some vacuously true statements are indeed true. If we were to declare all vacuously true statements as false, it would lead to undesirable consequences. For instance, if we accept that P → Q is true when both P and Q are true, and false when P is true but Q is false, then rejecting vacuous truth would make logical implication equivalent to logical conjunction (AND). This would blur the distinction between if and and, which are conceptually different. Furthermore, rejecting vacuous truth would force us to accept logically valid but counterintuitive arguments, such as concluding that P is true based solely on the logical connection between P and Q. Accepting vacuously true statements as true aligns with the axioms of propositional logic, which dictate that if P is false, then P → Q must be true. For many, these axioms are self-evidently truth-preserving, and rejecting them would undermine the validity of propositional calculus. However, some argue that only certain vacuously true statements should be considered true, as the connection between P and Q may not always be relevant. This objection is rooted in the idea of relevant logic, which requires a priori relevance between P and Q for the implication to hold. In mathematics, vacuous truths are common. For example, general statements about arbitrary sets must hold for all sets, including the empty set. For the empty set, such statements often reduce to vacuous truths. By accepting these vacuous truths as true, we avoid making exceptions for the empty set. Consider the property of being an antisymmetric relation: a relation R on a set S is antisymmetric if, for any a and b in S, a R b and b R a implies a = b. For the empty set, this property is vacuously true because there are no elements a and b to satisfy the condition. Another example is the theorem that states the empty set is a subset of any set X. This is equivalent to asserting that every element of the empty set is an element of X, which is vacuously true since the empty set has no elements. However, some vacuous truths are dismissed by mathematicians as nonsensical, even if they are technically true. For instance, generalizations of nonsensical statements can lead to vacuous truths that are not immediately apparent, potentially invalidating proofs if not handled carefully. In summary, vacuous truth is a logical construct that is often accepted as true to preserve the consistency and utility of logical and mathematical systems. While it may seem arbitrary or counterintuitive, rejecting vacuous truth can lead to significant complications. Nonetheless, vacuous truths provide no real information and are more a reflection of the logical framework than of any real-world fact.
